Summary

Executive Summary

Across the 4,330 jobs the shop released in 2025, gross margin ("margin": price less the job's full manufacturing cost, as a share of price) averaged 20% a job, with a standard deviation of 19 points, and 8% of jobs lost money; on revenue the year earned 24.3% against the 28.5% the jobs' estimates promised. Actual cost came in $1.67M over the jobs' estimates, 4.0% (96% of the cost measured): elements over estimate added $4.14M and elements under estimate took back $2.48M. Two cost elements carry most of the overrun: run hours ($651K) and outside processing ($617K). The largest named causes are revision work at one customer that was worked and never billed ($720K) and titanium and Inconel jobs that ran well past their estimated run hours ($460K); $1.11M has no cause the data can name. The decisions the owner took during the engagement act on causes that account for $1.74M, 42% of the $4.14M over estimate before offsets. The rest has no cause the data can name, sits in vendor prices and estimates no decision has reached yet, or is a cost the owner declined to act on; Section 9 lists the decisions both ways. What the job-level comparison showed, and the P&L could not, is that the year's 24.3% was an average of jobs running from a loss to well over 39%, and that the same part could do both in the same year.

Section 1

Job Margin Overview

The average 2025 job earned 20.4% margin against the 26.4% its estimate promised, and most jobs came in below their estimate. The P&L gave the shop one number: the jobs' $56.85M of revenue earned 24.3% against the 28.5% their estimates promised on the same revenue. The first chart shows how widely the jobs spread around the average: the red bars are the 363 jobs that lost money, 8% of jobs but only 4% of revenue, because the losing jobs are smaller than average. The second chart shows each job's actual margin less its estimated margin. 62% of jobs came in below their estimate, by a median of 10 points, while the jobs that beat their estimate did so by a median of 6; the red bars are the 15% of jobs more than 20 points below. The gap includes the price movement between quote and job as well as the jobs taking more than their estimates; Section 2 separates the two. Each bar is labeled with its number of jobs.

2025 Job Margin Distribution
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin

Repeat parts earn more than new quoted work but miss their estimates by more. Repeat parts average 23% a job and new quoted work 18%; on revenue, where the larger jobs count for more, they earn 27% and 20%. Both spread about as widely, and each loses money on 7% and 10% of its jobs, so no single pricing decision explains the spread. Against their estimates, repeat parts miss by an average of 7.1 points and new work by 4.1, with 17% of repeat jobs more than 20 points below against 12% of new ones. A repeat part's estimate comes from its original quote, so its gap carries every movement in material, rates and standards since then; a new part's estimate is weeks old. The panels in each chart share a scale.

2025 Job Margin, by Job Type
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin, by Job Type

Job size separates both the margin and the miss against estimate more sharply than job type does. Lots under 25 pieces average 10% a job and lose money on 23% of them; lots of 25 to 100 pieces average 22% and lose money on 5%, and lots over 100 pieces average 24% and lose money on 3%. The small lots also miss their estimates by the most: an average of 14.0 points, with 31% of them more than 20 points below, against 4.6 points for lots of 25 to 100 pieces and 2.9 for lots over 100. The setup costs the same whatever the lot, so a small lot carries it over fewer pieces, and Section 2.2 shows the setup itself runs over its standard on small lots, which the estimate does not carry. The panels count jobs on a common scale, and each bar is labeled with its number of jobs.

Section 2

Actual against Estimate

Every 2025 job's actual cost is set against its estimate, element by element: material, setup hours, run hours, outside processing, and scrap and rework, which the estimate does not carry. The estimate is first re-costed at the prices of the job's own day (its hours, as the estimate carried them, at the pool rate of the job's year; its material at the part's need at the job's issue price), so the labor elements compare hours and the material element compares usage. What prices moved since the quote is a pricing question, taken up in Section 7.

In margin terms: the estimates on the jobs promised 28.5% on the year's revenue. Re-costed at the prices of each job's own day they come to 27.2%, and the jobs earned 24.3%. The first 1.3 points are what material prices and labor rates moved between quote and job; the other 2.9 points are the jobs taking more than their estimates, and the rest of this section is about those.

Across the 4,330 jobs, actual cost came to $43.05M against a re-costed estimate of $41.38M: $1.67M over, 4.0% (96% of the cost measured). The net figure hides the two sides: elements over estimate added $4.14M, and elements under estimate took back $2.48M. Run hours and outside processing are the largest elements over estimate, followed by setup hours.

Section 2.1

Run hours over estimate

Run hours are over estimate almost everywhere a little, and in titanium and Inconel a lot. The little is stoppages: a job's run hours include the alarms and in-operation idle the machines record, 30% of machine time, and the routing standard carries no allowance for them. Standards set generously at first quote absorb part of it (before the refresh they sat a median 9% above the measured cycle), so the median job runs 1.09× its estimated run hours. Jobs in the two alloys ran 1.31× their estimated run hours in 2025 against 1.09× for every other material, and the gap shows on every cell that cuts them, which says the estimate is wrong rather than the floor: the estimator's speeds and feeds for the two alloys were never checked against a measured cycle. Across the 2025 jobs the excess over the shop's normal overrun comes to 2,193 hours and $460K across 209 jobs (99% of the cost measured). The action is to validate the two alloys' speeds and feeds against the measured cycles.

Two further causes sit in run hours. Parts whose routing standard was below the cycle the machines measured ran over the estimate by the difference until the standard was refreshed: $293K on 1,187 jobs. And the two oldest vertical mills, installed in 2006 and 2008, run the same program 1.26× as long as the newer ones on the 588 parts that ran on both; a job the schedule put on one of them carried that difference, $138K on 517 jobs.

Section 2.2

Setup hours over estimate

Setup overruns concentrate in small lots on the mill-turn and 5-axis cells. Measured at the cell against the routing standard, setup on lots under 25 pieces runs 1.62× the standard against 1.04× on larger lots: the standard assumes a repeat setup and a small lot gets a first-article setup every time. Margin by lot size shows the result, falling off sharply below 25 pieces rather than gradually.

Margin by Lot Size, with Setup Hours against Standard on the Mill-turn and 5-axis Cells, 2025

Across the 2025 jobs the setup excess on those cells comes to $46K across 147 jobs (98% of the cost measured); the first run after a revision adds $32K on 62 jobs, the same first-article effect on a part the shop already knew. The action is to quote small lots at the measured first-article setup.

Section 2.3

Labor hours over estimate with no routing cause

One customer's jobs run over on labor across every part family they buy. Mendoza-Davis jobs averaged 8.2 labor hours over estimate per job in 2025, against 0.3 for every other customer; in total they ran 1.27× their estimated hours against 1.01×. Nothing in the routing explains it: the excess shows on every part family the customer buys. The explanation is on the customer record. Mendoza-Davis issued 41 revision changes in the last twelve months against a median of 3 across the book, and each one adds programming and first-article time after release that was never billed.

Section 2.4

Outside processing over estimate

Outside processing over estimate has three parts. The plating vendor is the clearest case: it raised its prices in steps while the estimator's spreadsheet kept the old rate, so the gap between invoice and estimate widened quarter by quarter: on jobs whose only outside process is plating, the invoice ran 1.34× the estimate through 2025, and fell back to 1.03× once the quoting module carried the vendor's current price.

Plating: Invoice over Estimate by Quarter Released, Jobs Plated and Nothing Else

On the 2025 plated jobs that cost $88K. Other vendors' invoices above the estimate add more in total, $522K, but thinly: a median of $59 a job across 2,392 jobs, the drift of vendor prices since the job was quoted. The third part, $469K, is outside processing that could never be tied to a job and was spread over the month's jobs so the ledger reconciles; it is real money, but where it landed is an allocation, not a measurement. The action is to carry current vendor pricing in the quoting module; with a job number now required on every outside-processing purchase order, the comparison runs itself.

Section 2.5

Scrap and rework

Scrap material and rework hours cost the 2025 jobs $137K, led by stainless fittings ($20K) and turbine components ($18K). The figure is a floor: before the engagement most rework was posted as run time (881 events the audit found), so part of it sits in the run-hours line above and can only be partly separated after the fact.

Section 2.6

Material

Material usage is small, as it should be once issues are costed at their own price: $38K net across the 2025 jobs. What remains is the remnant and mis-issue cases the audit corrected (2,734 jobs that received another job's bar or never had theirs issued, brought back to the part's need).

Section 2.7

The overrun by cause

The same comparison, assigned to causes. Each element's overrun on each job goes to a named cause where the data shows one, sized as the excess over what a normal job of the year shows, and to "not attributable" where it does not. Elements that came in under their estimate are kept as an offset, so the table adds back to the net: the causes come to $4.14M over estimate before the $2.48M of elements under estimate bring it to $1.67M. It is a fact about 2025, not a promise about next year: the column does not total to anything recoverable. The cost-measured column is the coverage of the jobs behind each row; the outside processing allocated from the ledger is shown at 0% because it is an allocation.

Section 3

Same Part, Different Outcomes

For the 325 repeat parts with three or more jobs in 2025, the gap between each part's best and worst job has a median of 14 points; on 37% of them it is 20 points or more. Same part, same customer, same standing price, different outcome.

For quoting this means one thing: a part's price has to cover its worst realistic job, not its average. A standing price set on the typical lot on the newer machine loses money whenever the release is small, the schedule puts the job on an older mill or the customer revises the part, and each of those happens several times a year on the same part numbers.

Section 4

Jobs That Could Have Been Caught in Progress

The job in progress screen flags a job when its actual to date runs more than 15% over its estimate to date on labor hours, operation by operation, or on material at issue. Replayed over the 4,330 jobs completed from the 2025 releases, 1,279 would have been flagged, and 612 of them while there was still something to do: with operations left and 3 or more days before the job shipped. 33% of the flags fire at the first operation, where setup overruns show, 63% at a middle operation and 4% at the last, when only the next quote can change.

Where on the Routing the Flag Fired, 2025 Jobs

Grouped by what the shop could have done with the warning: on Mendoza-Davis's jobs a change order could have been raised before the work was done; on jobs that went on to ship late, a flag at the first operation leaves time to re-sequence rather than expedite; on small lots and first runs after a revision the quantity or scope could have been discussed with the customer. The three groups carried $1.29M of cost over estimate across 406 jobs. The rest were flagged too late or had no lever while open. The change-order figure is all cost over estimate on the jobs flagged while open, a different measure from the revision excess in Section 2.3.

Section 5

The Jobs That Lost Money

363 jobs lost money in 2025, $335,283 in total (97% of the cost measured). Set against their estimates, the losses are mostly not a pricing story: only 26 of the 363 were estimated to lose money before they started. The other 337 were estimated to make money, a median estimated margin of 23%, and lost it in the job; they carry 83% of the loss. Each job carries the driver the reporting layer assigns by rule, the same rules the Job Variance report applies to every job (appendix), and the action the driver maps to: correct the routing standard, correct the quote, bill the change order, reprice the part, fix the process, or accept it as a one-off. The top 25 are below; the full list is in the appendix. This is the list the owner and estimator work from, and it matches what they see in the ERP.

Section 7

Repricing

Exposure. At today's material prices, pool rates and measured standards, 246 of the 1,600 repeat parts (15%) have a standing price below current cost plus the shop's standard 28% markup (the markup price), carrying 12% of repeat revenue. The gap is modest on most of them: a median of 5.4%, with nine in ten under 15%; 4 sit below cost outright. At current volume the exposure is $256K a year, and the own-product line adds $326K: together 1.0% of 2025 revenue. Current cost rests on measured standards on 100% of the parts. The gap is what the annual across-the-board letters (3.0% to 3.5% a year) missed on the parts whose inputs moved most: since the last quote, current cost rose a median 21% on the parts below the markup price against 1% on the rest, while the letters raised the standing prices of those parts a median 11%.

What is defensible. In the shop's experience, as the owner and the controller described it, a routine annual increase of 3 to 5% is accepted without discussion. A larger increase can land selectively, part by part, when the cost driver is documented, and most often that driver is material passed through at what it now costs. Beyond that the relationship risk is real, and the owner decides.

Decisions. The controller and the owner decided every part below the markup price in weeks 7 to 9 on that basis: a gap within the routine range was repriced; a larger gap was repriced where material or outside processing drove it and the movement could be shown part by part, and held otherwise with the reason recorded; a large gap on a small part was exited, and on the 7 largest programs the increase was taken in two steps, half now and the balance at the blanket renewal.

Section 8

Estimate Accuracy

Estimate accuracy is the distribution of actual over estimate by cost element, for the 2025 history (estimates backfilled from the quoting module) and for the completed jobs of the engagement period (estimate carried on the job). This is the feedback loop the shop never had: the estimator can now see, element by element, whether the quotes were right.

Material moved to 1.00 and its spread closed because the estimate now carries the price of the day rather than the spreadsheet's price list. Setup hours have not moved yet (a median of 0.81 against 0.85): 40% of the engagement-period jobs were estimated before their part's refreshed standard took effect, and small lots still run over, which is what action A6 is for. Run hours narrowed from 0.97 to 1.28 to 1.02 to 1.24 because repeat parts are now estimated on the measured cycle. The median stays at 1.11 for a reason the refresh cannot fix: the measured cycle is time in cycle, while a job's run hours also carry the alarms and in-operation idle the machines record, 30% of machine time. The standard needs an allowance for them. Labor and burden tightened further because the estimate and the actual now use the same pool rate. Outside processing moved to 1.02 because the quoting module carries the vendors' current prices.

By estimator, the gap between the estimated margin and the margin runs 2 to 4 points, about the same for all three: the shortfall is in what the estimates carry, not in who writes them. By quote year, the margin on new work has not improved on its own, from 22% on work quoted in 2023 to 19% on work quoted in 2026; that is what the feedback loop is for.

Appendix

Method, Definitions and Detail

Job cost. Material at the issued price, corrected to the part's need where the audit found another job's bar or none; labor as hours at the work center's pool rate (labor rate × attended ratio + burden); outside processing at the invoiced price, with lines that could not be tied to a job allocated over the month's jobs; scrap at the job's material cost. CNC hours come from the machine-monitoring feed on every monitored cell, not from the clock record.

Measured share. The share of a job's cost resting on a transaction (a machine interval assigned to the job, a clock record, a scan, an issue, a purchase order) rather than on the routing standard, an allocated ledger residual or a record flagged unrepairable. Stated beside every dollar figure as the coverage of the jobs behind it.

Margin. Margin is gross margin: price less the job's cost (material, labor and burden at the work center's pool rate, outside processing and scrapped material), as a share of price. Estimated margin is the same measure on the job's estimate, and a job loses money when its margin is below zero. The shop prices as a markup on cost: its standard 28% markup, which the repricing queue in Section 7 uses, prices a job at cost × 1.28, a margin of 0.28 ÷ 1.28 = 21.9%. The charts in Section 1 show the average job.

Actual against estimate. Each job's actual cost less its estimate, with the estimate re-costed at the prices of the job's own day: its hours at the pool rate of the job's year, its material at the job's issue price. The difference splits exactly into the elements: material, setup hours, run hours, outside processing, and scrap and rework, which the estimate does not carry. A cause is sized as the excess over what a normal 2025 job shows: titanium and Inconel run hours beyond the median run ratio of other materials; small-lot and first-run setup beyond the median setup ratio of larger lots; Mendoza-Davis's hours beyond the shop's median labor ratio; the older mills' run hours times one less the ratio of newer to older cycle; standards below the measured cycle by the gap in the refresh log, on jobs estimated before the refresh.

Drivers. Section 5 assigns each job the driver the reporting layer's rules give it, the same rules the Job Variance report shows in the ERP: routing standard (run hours over 1.15× the estimate, and the part's other jobs in the trailing twelve months over too); small-lot setup (setup over 1.30× on a lot under 25 pieces); unbilled revision work (labor over estimate, a revision change after release and no change order billed); vendor rate (outside processing over 1.10× the estimate); scrap and rework (over 5% of estimated cost); material (over the estimate by more than 10%); priced below estimated cost (the job's own estimate showed a loss, sized as that estimated loss). Where several fire, the largest dollar variance is the driver; where none fires, or the largest carries under 40% of the job's overrun, the job is not attributable. The drivers are rules for a standing report and the Section 2 causes are an analysis of one year, so the two are close but not identical.

In-progress flag. A job is flagged at the first operation where its labor hours to date exceed the estimate to date by more than 15% and by at least two hours, or at the first material issue if material exceeds the estimate by more than 15% and $150. The estimate to date is the routing standard for each operation, scaled so the operations sum to the job's estimated hours. A flag is actionable when it fires before the last operation and 3 or more days before the job ships.
